newsitem.title: UK: IRA killers batter lingering N.Irish peace hopes.
newsitem.headline: IRA killers batter lingering N.Irish peace hopes.

text.p: Northern Ireland lurched into more instability on Tuesday after an IRA guerrilla attack killed two policemen and dealt a heavy blow to hopes for peace.
Britain broke off tentative contacts with the Irish Republican Army's political arm, Sinn Fein, as a result of the ambush and the United States and Ireland condemned the incident.
"The United States government too is outraged by the callous murder of two policemen in Northern Ireland," White House spokesman Mike McCurry told reporters on Monday.
"The IRA has claimed responsibility for what is ultimately an outrageous act of cowardice, an outrageous act of terrorism."

Sinn Fein chairman Mitchel McLaughlin expressed shock at the murders. "They diminish us all and I offer my condolences to the family." The IRA has been waging a guerrilla campaign since 1969 to end British rule in Northern Ireland.

Protestant and Catholic parties said the attack had been aimed at at deepening a centuries-old sectarian rift at a time of tension over impending pro-British street parades. Northern Ireland's Protestant majority favours continued rule by Britain.
Ireland and Britain said the IRA was trying to sabotage a peace initiative just when it might have made progress.
Politicians pleaded for no retaliation by pro-British Loyalists, fearing it would ignite simmering sectarian strife.
"It is a sad day for trying to move peace forward," said Mo Mowlam, Britain's Northern Ireland Secretary, after the daylight shootings. Both victims were married with young children.
Mowlam, who was scheduled to hold talks later on Tuesday about defusing sectarian conflict over a series of Protestant marches, urged "Loyalist" gunmen not to end an already shaky truce.

Revenge attacks would play into the IRA's hands, she warned, and lead to a spiral of death. "Those with those kind of emotions in their hearts tonight should think twice because they do nothing for anyone," she said on BBC television hours after the policemen were gunned down in Lurgan, a busy market town.
British Prime Minister Tony Blair, his face taut with anger, said the attack was callous and brutal.

"It is also something that has been designed to frustrate a process that was bringing hope to the people of Northern Ireland," he told television crews in Amsterdam where he was taking part in a European Union summit.
At his shoulder Irish Prime Minister John Bruton, grim faced and solemn, also condemned the double murder. In an interview later for Channel Four Television, he with scathing.
"I believe that Sinn Fein approves fully the activities of the IRA. I believe that Sinn Fein does the political bidding of the same leadership that leads the IRA and Sinn Fein."
Bertie Ahern, the Opposition leader who is expected to replace Bruton later this month following June 6 election successes, described the killing as evil and provocative.
Freddie Hall, Lurgan's police commander, told reporters the two officers were on routine town centre patrol.
"This type of slaying just numbs us all," he told reporters.

Politicians said the killing was a blatant attempt to inflame tension already building about a Protestant march that is due to go through an Irish Catholic enclave in the nearby town of Portadown on July 6. Britain fears that sectarian bickering could lead to a repeat of chaos that ensued last July.
Breandan Mac Cionnaith, leader of Catholic objectors, said they condemned the shootings. "No words can can express our horror and numb feelings at this act...We condemn the killings unreservedly."
